title: Answering why questions with because
keyIdea: A why question asks for a reason. 'Why is the dog wet?' does not want a place, like 'in the garden', or a thing, like 'a ball'. It wants what made it happen. So the answer starts with because: 'Because it jumped in the pond.' Saying because is not enough on its own. 'Because it is' and 'because I said so' do not say what made it happen, so they are not reasons. The reason goes after because, the right way round: 'There is a puddle because it rained', not 'It rained because there is a puddle'. When we do not know for sure, clues help us say why something might have happened: a plaster on a knee tells us she might be crying because she hurt it.
familyTip: Play 'I wonder why' on a walk or at bath time. Point at a puddle, a fallen leaf or a muddy boot and ask 'Why is it like that?'. Help your child start with because and give a reason they can see. Then swap, so they ask you a why question and check your answer.

visual.caption: Does it answer a why question? Drag each answer into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tell why from where, drag the cause into a because gap, sort real reasons, say them the right way round and use clues.

kid: Some questions start with why. Why is the dog wet? A why question wants a reason. It does not want a place, like in the garden. It wants to know what made it happen. So we start the answer with because. Because it jumped in the pond!
After because, say what made it happen. The ice cream melted because the sun was hot. The sun made it melt. Being pink or yummy did not.
Just saying because is not a reason. Because it is, or because I said so, does not tell us what made it happen. A real reason does. The floor is wet because I spilled my drink.

Say the reason the right way round. First it rained, then there was a puddle. So we say: there is a puddle because it rained. If we do not know for sure, we look for clues. A plaster on Mia's knee tells us she might be crying because she hurt it.
adult: Ages 4 to 5. This follows Development Matters (2021). At 3 to 4, children 'understand why questions'. In Reception they 'connect one idea or action to another' and use talk to explain 'why things might happen'. The Early Learning Goal for Speaking asks the same. Key words: why, because, reason, clue, might.

Why questions are harder than who, what and where questions. Blank, Rose and Berlin (1978) put them at the top level, because the child has to think past what they can see. So the lab first turns down place and thing answers. Then it moves to causes, non-reasons, word order and clues.

Common mistakes: giving a place or a name to a why question; thinking the word because makes any answer a reason, as in 'because it is'; putting the result after because, as in 'It rained because there is a puddle'; and giving a reason that does not fit, such as a colour or a day.

In the lab, children pick the answer that tells why. They drag the real cause into a because gap. They sort six answers into real reasons and not reasons. They tap the half of a sentence that is the reason, and a backwards sentence shows up as silly. Last, they tap the clue in a picture that tells them why.

practice.prompt: Answering why questions with because: why is the grass wet?
practice.hint: A why question wants a reason. Which answer starts with because?
practice.explain: Rain made the grass wet, so the answer is: because it rained. 'In the park' tells where, not why.

practice.prompt: Sam asks {n} why questions. Mum answers 1 of them with 'because I said so'. How many got a real reason?
practice.hint: 'Because I said so' is not a real reason, so take that one away.
practice.explain: {n} questions take away the 1 with no real reason leaves {=n-1} real reasons.

practice.prompt: Mia gives {n} reasons why her boots are muddy. Then she spots 1 more clue and gives 1 more reason. How many reasons now?
practice.explain: {n} reasons and 1 more make {=n+1} reasons. Clues help us find reasons.

practice.prompt: Ben says the window broke 'because it did'. Is that a reason?
choices: No, it does not say what broke it
Yes, it has because in it
Yes, it is a good reason
practice.hint: Does it tell you what made the window break?
practice.explain: 'Because it did' does not say what made it break. A real reason would be: because a ball hit it.

practice.prompt: Which one is the right way round?
choices: There is a puddle because it rained
It rained because there is a puddle
practice.hint: Which happened first: the rain or the puddle?
practice.explain: First it rained, then the puddle came. The reason, it rained, goes after because.

pool.hint: What makes snow turn into water?
pool.explain: The sun warmed the snow, so it melted. A hat cannot melt a snowman, and 'in the garden' tells where.

pool.prompt: Which word starts the answer to a why question?
pool.hint: Think of the word that comes before a reason.
pool.explain: We answer why with because, then the reason: because it was cold.

pool.prompt: Mum asks why you put your coat on. Which answer gives a real reason?
pool.hint: Which answer says what made you need a coat?
pool.explain: The cold made you need a coat, so 'because it is cold outside' is a real reason.

pool.prompt: The baby fell asleep. Which sentence says why, the right way round?
choices: The baby is asleep because she is tired
She is tired because the baby is asleep
pool.hint: Which comes first: being tired or falling asleep?
pool.explain: First the baby got tired, then she fell asleep. The reason goes after because.

pool.prompt: There are crumbs on Dad's beard and the cake is gone. Why might the cake be gone?
pool.hint: Look at the clue: where are the crumbs?
pool.explain: The crumbs on his beard are a clue, so the cake might be gone because Dad ate it.

pool.prompt: Gran answers {n} why questions. Each answer starts with because. How many times does she say because?
pool.hint: She says because once for each answer.
pool.explain: One because for each of the {n} answers makes {=n} times.

pool.prompt: Ella sorts {a} real reasons and {b} answers that are not reasons. How many answers did she sort?
pool.hint: Put the two groups together and count them all.
pool.explain: {a} and {b} make {=a+b} answers. Only the {a} real reasons say what made it happen.

pool.prompt: Why is the dog wet? Which answer tells WHY?
choices: Because it jumped in the pond
pool.hint: A why answer gives a reason, not a place or a thing.
pool.explain: Jumping in the pond made the dog wet. 'In the garden' tells where and 'a brown dog' tells what.

pool.prompt: Why did the ice lolly drip?
choices: Because it was on a stick
pool.hint: What makes ice turn to water?
pool.explain: Warmth melts ice, so the lolly dripped because it got warm. Its colour and its stick did not make it drip.
